content:
Guinness is a world-class example of consistency AND coherence

Last week at the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) Effectiveness Conference, Orlando Wood shared his POV on brand coherence with System1 and The Whole-Brained Marketer. It’s an important addition to the consistency conversation, and Guinness is a brilliant way to explain why.

Conveniently, I own the T-shirt. One of my favourites!

Guinness has used the harp since 1862. Look at how much it has changed without becoming something else entirely. Consistency leaves plenty of room for creativity when you understand what’s worth keeping.

What I particularly love is that, after years of simplification, the 2016 redesign brought back detail and craftsmanship. Design Bridge and Partners worked with Gerry Barney, who drew the 1968 version, along with harp-makers and a letterpress studio. A more thoughtful brief than “make it work as an app icon.”

That's where consistency meets coherence. The craftsmanship in the identity belongs with the care in the pour, the anticipation of the first sip, and the beer's character. The design reinforces the experience. It gives the familiar symbol more meaning.

Orlando shared Paul Simonet's framework, which looks at a brand’s heart, face, voice, and actions. What it stands for, how it looks, how it communicates and what it does should add up to a recognisable character. That goes well beyond advertising; it's part of the brand strategy process.

You can put the same logo on five unrelated ideas and still have five unrelated ideas.

This new initial, exploratory study of 21 IPA award-winning brands found that brands whose coherence improved (consistently delivered across Paul's framework over time) were more likely to report effects: a small study, but an interesting direction for the industry to pay attention to.

This builds on the case for consistency. My 'Compound Creativity' work over the past 4 years with the IPA, System1 and Effie Worldwide found that the most consistent UK and US brands reported an average ROI of 8.8, versus 2.1 for the least consistent. There is considerable commercial value associated with building on what you’ve already established.

There's now significant empirical evidence for what marketers have always known is best practice.

COHERENT BRANDS: Be clear on who your brand is, what it stands for, and what it looks like. Make sure the brand lives up to this across its products, partnerships, communications and customer experience.

CONSISTENT CAMPAIGNS: Give good campaign ideas time to develop. Keep building the assets, characters and associations people recognise. 

We need both. The person buying a pint doesn’t care whether something came from the brand team, the social agency or the partnerships team. It’s all Guinness to them.

Links to both pieces of research in the comments.

content:
Sooo... a little announcement from today.

It's been one year at Shake. And what a year it’s been  🙌 

A year ago, I left LinkedIn to join a small agency with big ambitions. Since then, we have grown, launched things, worked with brilliant people and had a lot of fun along the way.

The question I’ve been asked most is: “What’s it like going from a huge company to a small one?”

So I wanted to share a few reflections for anyone considering a similar move.

First, this comes from someone who loves LinkedIn. I’m a proud former employee and ambassador, and I’ve always said it’s an AMAZING company to work for. I miss many things about my time there, especially the people.

These are personal observations about my own experience, rather than a verdict on where anyone else should work.

1) Autonomy suits me
I like having room to make decisions, try things and take responsibility for what happens next. I’m usually happier testing an idea than spending weeks discussing whether we should test it.

Big companies have more people and priorities to account for. I understand why. But I’ve realised how much I enjoy working somewhere that moves at my pace.

2) I spend less time proving I’m doing the work
In a large organisation, doing good work and making sure the right people know about it can become two separate jobs.

3) I have become more comfortable being myself here
My LinkedIn content has become funnier, occasionally more unhinged, and a lot more enjoyable to create. I have tried new angles, made more jokes and explored commercial opportunities I probably wouldn’t have pursued before.

4) Ideas have somewhere to go
An idea can become something people actually use within days. We’ve launched parody tools, our Best Time to Post tool and the What Just Happened Podcast. Some ideas start as a business opportunity. Others start with “this would be funny”.

I really like having the ownership to follow that curiosity and help build the thing.

5) The impact feels closer
You see a conversation turn into a client. You see someone use a tool you helped launch. You see how your work contributes to the business growing. I cared deeply about my work at LinkedIn too. At a smaller company, the connection is just easier to see and feel.

6) You have to enjoy things changing
More meetings out of the office, different challenges each week, priorities moving as opportunities come in. That can be messy. It also suits me. I’ve learned that variety gives me energy, even when it makes the calendar slightly ridiculous.

If you are considering a similar move, think about the conditions in which you do your best work. How much structure do you want? How comfortable are you with uncertainty? What gives you energy?

This year has helped me answer those questions for myself.

A huge thank you to the whole Shake Content team, especially James Farnfield and Harry Williams, for the trust, support, guidance and room to run with things.

It’s been a brilliant year. Here’s to many more ✌️

Want to know how to be a successful creator?

This is one of those killer charts from System1 that shows you how it works

With so much content out there how do you make sure that yours connects with the audience and is remembered in the future? After all the point is to make sure your brand comes to mind when someone is thinking about buying

PUTTING ON A SHOW

Orlando Wood has been championing Showmanship for some years now and brilliantly demonstrates how right brain features in advertising are more likely to create an emotion and lodge into memory than left brain ones.

See the chart for examples of this in the top right box and you'll immediately see why your favourite creators are so successful - they love to put on a show

BRAND x CREATOR IMPACT

I think one of the biggest gaps in capability right now is how brands work with creators. The temptation to use them as a media channel rather than a creative partner. Even on Uncensored CMO I have experienced this gap first hand and it leads to a loss in effectiveness

This report really helps provide the evidence to brands for how they can get the most out of creator partnerships 

THE POWER OF SURPRISE

Adam Morgan and I used a version of this chart for our Startling Power of Surprise talk at Cannes to show how being surprising is the most potent way to create a positive memory. if you want to geek out on this then look up 'reward prediction error'.

If you look at the size of the bubbles you'll see that something out of the ordinary has the greatest impact on brand memory

With so much money being invested in creators you can't afford to get this wrong

Kudos to Andrew Tindall Josh Fruttiger & Beth Marchant and their partners TikTok for Business & WPP Media for pulling such rich insights together

content:
A while back I gave a talk in London, and at the end I opened the floor to questions.

A man with a friendly face and wise eyes put his hand up and asked, "When you started presenting Formula 1, who was kind to you?"

Nobody had asked me that in all the years since I started the job. What a lovely way to ask about such a big moment in my life.

I hate the phrase "self-made man". I've never met one. When I got the BBC F1 job I was far from alone. Niall, my boss, put his arm around me. Mark the producer gave me years of wisdom. David and Eddie, my pundits, gave me the confidence to stand shoulder to shoulder with them on TV.

And still it was lonely. The contract was 12 months. I knew I was a risk for the BBC, and that one misstep could cost me the job and maybe my whole career. I was young for it, and the next hour felt like it would decide everything.

The loneliest moment came about 10 minutes before we went live in Australia. I walked away from David and Eddie and stood on my own in a pretty empty pit lane. Ear defenders on, six or seven voices in my head, the PA counting down, no autocue, and one voice telling me I was about to mess it up.

With about five minutes to go I couldn't take any more. I took my earpiece out and made a call. When it was answered, all I said was, "I'm scared Dad."

My parents were up early at their cottage in the Norfolk countryside, ready to watch their son host live TV on BBC One. Only a few years before, their boy had been struggling with life and not much was expected of him. I still get emotional thinking about what they said next.

"We're having tea and toast, it's still dark, and the dog is curled up on the floor. Life here is exactly the same as it always has been, and you can always come home. No matter what happens today we love you, always will, and our door will never close. So go and enjoy yourself, knowing that."

My life had changed, but life itself hadn't. Knowing I could just go home, no judgement, no failure, lifted the weight completely.

I put the earpiece back in, listened to the minutes tick down, and went live to millions.

Who was kind to you when it really mattered? It might be worth telling them ❤️

content:
💾Gabriel Davis at Anthropic published data analysing 2.5M+ Instagram posts, and the numbers are pretty crazy.

Between Jan 2025 and May 2026:
1) Likes dropped 73% for carousels and 81% for reels
2) Comments fell 39% to 46% across the board
3) Even top 1% accounts saw 50-65% drops in engagement

My take: Instagram is increasingly built for passive consumption and private sharing. 

LinkedInis moving in the exact opposite direction. It is s becoming more conversational.

Active discourse and comment sections have become the real engine for reach, authority, and pipeline.

Yes, AI has also created an supply of generic posts and painfully predictable comments. But the growing importance of the comment section is still an encouraging signal.

LinkedIn isn’t rewarding people for simply consuming content. It’s creating more value around people contributing to it. 

The future of LinkedIn may belong less to the people with the biggest audiences, and more to those who start the best conversations.

content:
One of the most underrated things in content is being recognisable.

I have spent years working with founders, executives and brands on LinkedIn, and it's something I come back to constantly.

Think about the people and companies you instantly recognise in your feed. Sometimes you don't even need to see their name to know who's behind the content.

Their personality, their style, the way they communicate. All of that builds familiarity over time. And familiarity is a big part of how trust is built.

Which is why I find Synthesia's latest launch quite cool.

They've just introduced Syren, which lets you generate videos from a prompt using your existing brand identity.

You upload existing videos as Brand Context, and Syren learns things like motion, pacing, tone of voice, colours and fonts.

Then you give it a prompt, and it creates a new video using that context.

Pretty impressive when you see it in action.

We've spent years talking about the importance of building a recognisable brand. But maintaining that identity across different channels, formats and types of content takes a lot of work.

Technology that helps teams carry that identity into more of what they produce is genuinely interesting.

Especially as video becomes an increasingly important part of how brands communicate.

Of course, the ideas, creative direction and understanding of your audience still matter enormously. Those are the foundations of good content, regardless of how it's produced.
But I love seeing how tools like this are expanding what's possible for creative and marketing teams.

content:
Don't just quit without thinking about it!

Most people think going fractional means quitting full time. It doesn't.

Some of the people I see doing this best are still in full-time jobs. 

They're not ready to jump, and they don't need to be. 

They're doing it alongside their day job — for extra income, to test the waters, to chase something they actually care about!

Full-time or fractional isn't a real dichotomy. You can do both.

And fractional work compounds exactly like everything else. 

The reps you put in this year are the reason you'll have options in three or four years — a client base, a reputation, a safety net you built before you needed one.

If any of this makes you nervous, that's exactly the signal to start.

content:
Audio makes up almost a quarter of the UK's media day, yet most brands' media plans leave it out, and few have a distinctive audio brand asset. What gives?

I know there's huge opportunity in social, creator, and connected media right now. But we can't forget audio's incredible power.

In my research with Mark Ritson shared at Cannes this year, the Effie Worldwide data revealed that campaigns with audio in their plans see a 23% increase in the total reported brand and business effects on average.

It's not causal research; we can't claim audio CAUSES more outcomes. But when you see research like this, it becomes pretty obvious that not including audio as a touchpoint in a campaign is us sleeping on a big opportunity to reach more customers more regularly, to change more behaviour in brands' favour.

content:
Selfies on LinkedIn can lead to more opportunities. I know. I’m still a bit conflicted.

Business Insider just covered creators using selfies and unscripted videos to build an audience, get speaking invitations and even land jobs.

Having spent 4+ years at LinkedIn working closely with creators, I have seen how much it helps when people get to know the person behind the posts. A face adds familiarity. A personal story gives people something to connect with beyond a job title.

And with so much AI content around, I understand the appetite for something that feels more human.

But I’m less enthusiastic about the takeaway becoming: “Attach a selfie. Get more reach.”

A random selfie attached to an unrelated business lesson because someone told you it performs better? That’s where you lose me.

I have always liked the idea of “personality yes, personal optional.” You should be able to build a reputation through your ideas and expertise without feeling obliged to put your face on every post.

I use photos of myself too, so this is also a question for me: how much is helping people get to know you, and how much is fishing for attention?

Where do you land? Do selfies make you more interested in someone’s content, or does it depend on what they have to say?

content:
We've done it again.

Outgrown a London HQ that was supposed to last.

Five offices in six years. I can tell you exactly who we were in each one.

Call me a romantic but I get strangely nostalgic when it comes to thinking about office moves 

Six years ago, I was alone at a desk.

Five years ago, hot desks at Huckletree in Shoreditch. Six of us.

Four years ago, our first dedicated office. 12 people, Hammersmith, no windows. My least favourite of them all. 

Three years ago, Brick Lane. 30 people in a space built for way fewer. We stayed too long, outgrew it fast, and spilled into every common space in the building — much to our neighbours' annoyance.

Two years ago, our first proper serviced office. 45 people, a roof terrace. The first place that actually felt like home.

Now an office for 60. We've outgrown it just as fast.

Every move's meant letting go of whatever stopped working — the processes, the habits, sometimes the people — and building for who we needed to become next.

We think we've found the next one. 

This one feels right, the way the good ones always have.

Watch this space.

When I visited Toto Wolff at Mercedes HQ, he was keen to show me a picture he'd had put up on the wall.

It commemorates every F1 title winner since 1958, which is special enough on its own. What makes it really special is that it also has 24 blank spaces, one for each of the next 24 winners.

His message to the team is that they won't win all 24, but history hasn't been written yet, and they're the ones who will write it.

I love that as a way to lead. Whatever you've already achieved, the next space on the wall is still blank 💥
